All broken launches at a glance

CaseFirst error afterWhat you seeGoverned by
Slurm: node missing602 snothing for 600 s, then a bare RendezvousTimeoutErrortorchrun c10d join timeout, 600 s
Kubernetes: pod missing903 snothing for 900 s, then "1/2 clients joined"torchrun static store timeout, 900 s (launcher default)
Ray: worker unplaceable60 s"worker group startup timed out" every minuteRay Train worker-group start timeout, 60 s, then retried forever
Kubernetes: short host name902 spod 1: gai warnings; pod 0: "1/2 clients joined" after 900 storchrun static store timeout, 900 s
Slurm: typo in address162 sgai warnings, then "timed out after 60000ms"c10d store client read_timeout, 60 s (took longer)
Slurm: localhost601 snothing for 600 s, then RendezvousTimeoutErrorc10d join timeout, 600 s
Slurm: port collision601 s"Did the remote server shutdown or crash?"the other job's join timeout, 600 s
Slurm: wrong WORLD_SIZE121 s"wait timeout after 120000ms, keys: /default_pg/0//cpu//0/0"process-group timeout (120 s here; 30 min default)
Kubernetes: rank stuck60 ssend and recv timeouts, and a misleading "remote worker crashing"process-group timeout (60 s here; 30 min gloo, 10 min NCCL default)

Each case ran once (the times are set by timeouts, so they repeat: two independent 600 s cases gave 601 and 602 s, two 900 s cases 902 and 903 s). Every waiting process held its CPUs and (fake) GPUs the whole time. On a real cluster, multiply by the allocation: a 64-node, 512-GPU job that loses one node before the rendezvous idles 512 × 10 min = 85 GPU-hours before torchrun says anything (calculation).
tools:
1. Where is each process right now? py-spy dump

py-spy reads a running Python process's stack from outside, without stopping it. In Kubernetes the pod has no permission to trace other processes (the VM's ptrace_scope is 1 and pods lack CAP_SYS_PTRACE), so it ran from the node, against the pod's process ID as the node sees it, 15 s after the stall began:

rank 3 (the stalled one)
    train (train.py:166)
    main (la_probe.py:67)
    <module> (la_probe.py:81)
train.py:166 is time.sleep(a.slow_ms / 1000): the injected stall.
rank 0 (one of the waiting ones)
    _pre_forward (torch/nn/parallel/distributed.py:1776)
    forward (torch/nn/parallel/distributed.py:1887)
    _call_impl (torch/nn/modules/module.py:1794)
    _wrapped_call_impl (torch/nn/modules/module.py:1783)
    train (train.py:154)
    main (la_probe.py:67)
    <module> (la_probe.py:81)
Inside DDP's forward: step 2 begins by rebuilding gradient buckets, which broadcasts across ranks and waits for rank 3. Rank 2 was inside backward (train.py:156), also blocked on a collective.

On a real job you would run it on a handful of ranks (py-spy dump --pid, add --native for C++ frames): the outlier stack is the answer.

2. Who is behind? The flight recorder

PyTorch keeps a ring buffer of each rank's last collectives (2,000 by default, TORCH_FR_BUFFER_SIZE), with a sequence number per process group; in torch 2.14 gloo records into it too (FlightRecorder.hpp:110). The probe dumped it with torch._C._distributed_c10d._dump_fr_trace_json() when a rank failed, and on SIGUSR1 for the sleeping rank 3:

RankLast collectiveIts nameAll recorded (sequence number, kind)
rank 0#7gloo:broadcast#1 all_gather, #2 broadcast, #3 broadcast, #4 all_reduce, #5 all_reduce, #6 broadcast, #7 broadcast
rank 1#6gloo:broadcast#1 all_gather, #2 broadcast, #3 broadcast, #4 all_reduce, #5 all_reduce, #6 broadcast
rank 2#8gloo:all_reduce#1 all_gather, #2 broadcast, #3 broadcast, #4 all_reduce, #5 all_reduce, #6 broadcast, #7 broadcast, #8 all_reduce
rank 3#5gloo:all_reduce#1 all_gather, #2 broadcast, #3 broadcast, #4 all_reduce, #5 all_reduce

Rank 3 stopped at #5 (the loss all-reduce of step 1); every other rank had issued #6 or later. The rank with the lowest sequence number is the one the others are waiting for. #1 to #3 are DDP's start-up (shape check, then broadcasting rank 0's weights), #4 the gradient all-reduce, #5 the running example's loss all-reduce, #6 onwards step 2. With NCCL the same dump is written automatically on a timeout when TORCH_NCCL_DUMP_ON_TIMEOUT=1; PyTorch ships a torchfrtrace analyser that compares the dumps of all ranks.

3. More logs: TORCH_DISTRIBUTED_DEBUG and NCCL_DEBUG documented

TORCH_DISTRIBUTED_DEBUG=INFO or DETAIL makes DDP log its bucketing and unused parameters; DETAIL also wraps every collective with a check that all ranks call the same collective with the same shapes, and reports the mismatch instead of hanging, at a cost in speed (use it to reproduce, not in production). NCCL_DEBUG=INFO (section 6) shows which interface and transport each rank chose, which is where most GPU start-up hangs are found. TORCH_CPP_LOG_LEVEL=INFO shows the store's connect and retry messages seen in the cases above.

The Service JobSet created, named after the JobSet: no virtual IP (clusterIP: None), and it publishes pods that are not ready yet.
pod spec (set by JobSet):
  hostname:  la-t1-node-0-1
  subdomain: la-t1

getent hosts la-t1-node-0-0.la-t1   (in pod 1)
<ip-1>     la-t1-node-0-0.la-t1.mi.svc.cluster.local
search mi.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local
Pod 1 resolved pod 0's name at its own start-up, 0.08 s before pod 0's torchrun had even begun: the name exists as soon as the pod has an address. ndots:5 and the search list are why the short form la-t1-node-0-0.la-t1 works inside the namespace.
pgtext: Measured here, with 4 ranks on 2 containers: init_process_group over gloo took a median 9 ms on Slurm, 26 ms on Kubernetes and 333 ms on Ray (measured on Apple M1 Pro, Docker Desktop VM, shared machine; on Ray it includes waiting for the slowest worker to arrive, since Ray Train calls it in all workers at once). It is fast because every rank was already waiting at the store: the expensive part of start-up is getting every process to that point, and on GPUs, NCCL's own bootstrap and topology detection after it.

drills.q: Ten minutes after submission the job log shows only this. What happened?
drills.log:
job 72 nodes c[1-2] rendezvous c1:29500
torch.distributed.elastic.rendezvous.api.RendezvousTimeoutError
srun: error: c1: task 0: Exited with exit code 1
srun: error: c2: task 1: Terminated
opts: The rendezvous port 29500 is blocked by a firewall
Node c2 never started its torchrun (or never reached the store), so c1 waited the full 600 s join timeout
The model ran out of memory on c1
drills.ans: A port blocked by a firewall would show connection warnings on c2, which logged nothing at all. Nothing from c2 plus a join timeout on c1 means c2's agent never joined: look at c2's own task (here it was sleeping on purpose).

drills.q: Pod 1 of a JobSet logs this over and over. What is wrong?
drills.log: [c10d] The IPv6 network addresses of (la-badaddr-node-0-0, 29500) cannot be retrieved (gai error: -2 - Name or service not known).
opts: The rendezvous address is the pod's short host name; it resolves only inside pod 0. Use the name under the headless Service (la-badaddr-node-0-0.la-badaddr)
IPv6 is disabled in the cluster
drills.ans: gai error -2 is a name that does not resolve. The kubelet puts a pod's own short name in its /etc/hosts, so the name works in pod 0 and nowhere else; cluster DNS knows <hostname>.<subdomain>. The IPv6 wording is just the first address family tried.

drills.q: Three ranks print this after exactly the process-group timeout. Which rank do you investigate?
drills.log:
rank 0 (+60.0 s): RuntimeError: [/__w/pytorch/pytorch/third_party/gloo/gloo/transport/tcp/pair.cc:561] Connection closed by peer [<ip-5>]:11167. This is typically caused by a remote worker crashing. Check the logs of the remote worker before reporting an error. GLHF! 🏖️
rank 1 (+60.0 s): RuntimeError: [/__w/pytorch/pytorch/third_party/gloo/gloo/transport/tcp/unbound_buffer.cc:129] Timed out waiting 60000ms for send operation to complete
rank 2 (+60.0 s): RuntimeError: [/__w/pytorch/pytorch/third_party/gloo/gloo/transport/tcp/unbound_buffer.cc:78] Timed out waiting 60000ms for recv operation to complete
opts: Rank 0: it reports a crashed remote worker
Rank 3: it is the only one that printed nothing; check where it is (py-spy) and the flight recorder's sequence numbers
drills.ans: Every message here is a symptom. The silent rank is the suspect: in this run py-spy showed it sleeping in train.py:166 and the flight recorder showed it one collective behind all others.

drills.q: Two ranks of a three-task srun job fail with this after 120 s. Cause?
opts: WORLD_SIZE says 4 but only 3 processes exist: they wait for rank 3's address
The store on rank 0 is overloaded
drills.ans: The key is the store entry where gloo's rank 3 would post its address; nobody ever writes it. Read WORLD_SIZE from the launcher (SLURM_NTASKS) instead of hard-coding it.
